strengths: The paper is well-motivated: it identifies a genuine gap (implicit mechanisms in modern SSMs like Mamba) and proposes a coherent research program for making analogous mechanisms explicit within the interpretable HiPPO polynomial framework.

Each of the five extensions is grounded in solid, non-trivial mathematical derivations (e.g., the time-warping equivalence for Salience HiPPO, the Volterra kernel parameterization in OP bases, the Jacobi-matrix/arcsine-law argument for why naive Jeffreys-style multiscale reweighting fails, and the reduced-rank-regression induced geometry for Forecasting HiPPO). These derivations are careful and largely self-contained.

The experimental design directly targets and isolates the claimed capability for each extension (e.g., quadratic Volterra kernel recovery, selective copying for salience, associative recall for key-value memory, variable-horizon reconstruction for multiscale), and the synthetic tasks are simple enough that the resulting visualizations (history measures, output functionals, kernel maps) convincingly demonstrate the intended interpretable mechanism.

The paper includes an unusually honest and informative evaluation beyond the toy settings: a character-level WikiText-2 language modeling comparison (Section 3.6) that quantifies the interpretability-performance trade-off, including a reported failure case (Associative Memory HiPPO at 20.41 PPL) rather than cherry-picking only favorable results.

Extensive appendix material (full experimental protocols, closed-form update derivations, scaling ablations for baselines in Table 3) supports reproducibility and pre-empts the objection that baselines were simply undertrained or under-parameterized.
weaknesses: The five 'zoo' members are fairly disparate mechanisms unified mainly by narrative rather than a single technical framework; there is no experiment combining multiple extensions together (e.g., salience + associative memory + multiscale in one model), so it remains unclear whether these mechanisms compose or trade off against each other in a realistic architecture.

Evaluation is almost entirely on small, hand-designed synthetic tasks that appear tailored to showcase each specific mechanism (e.g., selective copying with uniform allocation patterns, associative recall with clean binary key/value alternation). This risks favoring the proposed models by construction and limits confidence that the demonstrated advantages would hold on less curated or longer-range real-world tasks.

The only real-data evaluation (character-level WikiText-2, single/two-layer models) shows all HiPPO Zoo variants underperforming modern SSMs by substantial margins (e.g., 6.80–20.41 PPL vs. 4.65–5.75 for SSM baselines), and one variant fails catastrophically; this substantially limits the paper's claim of practical significance beyond a purely diagnostic/interpretability tool.

Volterra HiPPO's O(N^k) scaling for order-k interactions is acknowledged as a serious practical limitation but is not empirically addressed (e.g., no experiments with the proposed low-rank tensor approximation), leaving open how well the approach would scale beyond second order.

Originality is somewhat incremental: individual components (Volterra series, time-warped ODEs, key-value associative memory, log-scale multiscale representations, reduced-rank regression for forecasting) are well-established techniques from classical signal processing/statistics; the contribution is primarily their re-formulation within the HiPPO polynomial-coefficient framework rather than fundamentally new algorithmic ideas.

There is no quantitative measure of 'interpretability' itself (e.g., human evaluation, downstream probing utility); claims of interpretability rest on qualitative visualizations, which, while illustrative, are not rigorously validated against alternative explanation methods for standard SSMs.

strengths: The paper offers a genuinely interesting reframing of several modern SSM capabilities (nonlinear interactions, adaptive memory, associative recall, multiscale representation, and forecasting-induced memory) as explicit, interpretable modifications of the HiPPO measure/dynamics rather than opaque learned gating.

Some of the theoretical connections are elegant and non-trivial, e.g., the time-warping equivalence for Salience HiPPO (Eq. 3-5), the Volterra-kernel-in-OP-basis derivation, and the arcsine-law argument (via Kuijlaars & Van Assche) explaining why naive Jeffreys-weighted scale embeddings fail to change effective timescale coverage.

The appendices are unusually thorough, providing full experimental configurations (architectures, learning rates, discretization schemes, closed-form update rules) that substantially aid reproducibility.

The authors run non-trivial scaling ablations for baselines (Table 3), showing they made an effort to give baselines a fair chance (e.g., testing 10x capacity/data/steps and positional embeddings for transformers/LSTMs) rather than using undertrained strawmen.

The paper is reasonably honest about negative results, e.g., explicitly reporting that Associative Memory HiPPO performs catastrophically (20.41 PPL) on language modeling and discussing this as a genuine mismatch rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: Central motivating claim is not well supported: despite framing the work around 'explicit' analogues of Mamba's capabilities, Mamba is never included as a baseline on the synthetic selective-copying and associative-recall tasks (Table 1/3) that are precisely the tasks Mamba/H3-style papers were designed to solve, so the comparison to what 'modern SSMs' actually achieve on these benchmarks is missing.

The only real-data evaluation (character-level WikiText-2, Section 3.6) shows all five HiPPO Zoo variants clearly underperforming even simple parameter-matched baselines (LSTM, S4D, Mamba), with gaps of 23-36% in perplexity and one variant failing outright (20.41 vs 5.54 PPL for Mamba). This substantially undercuts the paper's claim that 'capabilities typically associated with modern SSMs can be realized through explicit, interpretable polynomial memory structures,' since realization is only demonstrated on hand-designed toy tasks and fails to transfer to real sequential data.

The five 'zoo' members are not really unified beyond sharing the HiPPO substrate; each has its own bespoke architecture, task, and evaluation protocol, and none of the experiments combine two or more extensions together, so the 'unified framework' framing is more aspirational than demonstrated.

Each synthetic task (selective copying, associative recall, variable-horizon reconstruction, quadratic Volterra system, GP forecasting) appears custom-designed to closely match the corresponding mechanism, raising concerns about whether these results generalize beyond the specific toy settings constructed for each extension.

Volterra HiPPO's parameter count grows as O(N^k), which the paper acknowledges is a serious scalability bottleneck without providing empirical evidence that the proposed low-rank tensor mitigation actually works.

Interpretability claims rely primarily on qualitative visualizations (e.g., Figures 1-6) rather than any quantitative interpretability metric, making it hard to assess how much genuine mechanistic insight is gained versus how much is post hoc narrative around plots.
The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate ('none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted') and does not engage with any specifics of the work, even superficially.

No comparison to established long-range benchmarks (e.g., Long Range Arena) or larger-scale settings is provided, limiting confidence that the observed advantages/trade-offs would hold outside small synthetic and small-scale char-LM settings.

strengths: The paper introduces a coherent and well-motivated unifying perspective: recasting five distinct modern SSM capabilities (nonlinearity, adaptive/selective memory, associative recall, multiscale representation, forecasting-induced memory) as explicit, interpretable modifications to the HiPPO history measure or readout, rather than opaque learned dynamics.

Each extension is grounded in solid theory: Volterra kernels naturally expressed in OP coefficients, a clean time-warping interpretation for Salience HiPPO with an explicit induced history measure, a principled minimum-norm/kernel-based associative write rule, a Jacobi-matrix argument for why log-timescale embedding (vs. naive polynomial-in-g or Jeffreys weighting) is needed for genuine multiscale coverage, and a rigorous derivation connecting forecasting objectives to an induced quadratic form/geometry on histories via reduced-rank regression.

Empirical validation is reasonably thorough for a mechanism-focused paper: multiple synthetic tasks per extension, visual diagnostics (induced measures, kernels, eigenfunctions) that directly substantiate the interpretability claims, and parameter-matched comparisons against LSTM/S4D/Transformer baselines.

Notable honesty in evaluation: additional scaling/ablation studies (Appendix C.6, Table 3) probing whether baselines could match performance with more capacity/data/steps/positional embeddings, and a forthright WikiText-2 comparison showing HiPPO Zoo variants underperform modern SSMs (including a reported catastrophic failure of Associative Memory HiPPO), which strengthens rather than undermines credibility.
Reproducibility is strong: extensive appendices detail exact architectures, discretization schemes, hyperparameters, training protocols, and mathematical derivations for every experiment.
weaknesses: All quantitative evidence comes from small synthetic tasks (and one small character-level LM benchmark); there is no evaluation at a scale or on real tasks that would establish whether these mechanisms retain their claimed advantages (or even remain tractable, given e.g. O(N^k) Volterra scaling) in realistic settings.

The five "zoo" members are evaluated entirely in isolation; no experiments combine two or more extensions (e.g., salience + associative memory, as real Mamba-like models effectively must integrate several such capabilities simultaneously), leaving open whether the mechanisms compose or interfere.

The paper's own analysis (Appendix D.4) concedes that Multiscale HiPPO is not more expressive than a bank of independent HiPPO systems, just a more compact/queryable parameterization — this weakens the novelty claim for that component specifically.

The synthetic tasks (selective copying, associative recall) are somewhat hand-designed to align with the proposed mechanism's structure (e.g., "uniform allocation patterns across state dimensions" is explicitly noted as a favorable condition for Salience HiPPO), so it's unclear how much the strong synthetic results generalize beyond curated settings; the WikiText-2 results, where gaps to Mamba are 23-36% and one variant fails catastrophically, are consistent with this concern.

No comparison to other interpretable/structured memory or SSM approaches beyond the HiPPO lineage and standard black-box baselines (LSTM/S4D/Transformer/Mamba), making it hard to situate the contribution relative to other interpretability-oriented sequence modeling work.
The impact statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with implications of the work.
